claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi and closely matched high-entropy derivatives have high saturation magnetization.
Untreated single-phase fcc FeCoNi and its reported high-entropy derivatives have coercive fields around or below 100 Oe.
Controlled low-temperature isothermal aging of fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative will induce nanoscale decomposition or precipitation.
The aging-induced nanoprecipitates will be finely dispersed within the fcc matrix.
Aging temperature can be selected to promote spinodal decomposition.
A sufficiently low aging temperature will limit precipitate coarsening.
The aging treatment can produce nanoprecipitates without causing a complete transformation of the fcc matrix.
The nanoprecipitates will act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning of magnetic domain walls by the nanoprecipitates will increase coercivity.
Aged samples will have a coercive field significantly above approximately 100 Oe relative to untreated samples.
The coercivity increase can be achieved while largely retaining the high saturation magnetization.
The coercivity improvement will depend on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Excessive precipitate volume or coarsening may compromise saturation magnetization or overall magnetic properties.
Keeping the composition similar to FeCoNi will help preserve high magnetization and the fcc matrix.
Room-temperature hysteresis measurements on identically processed aged and untreated samples can determine whether aging changes coercivity and saturation magnetization.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls for nanoprecipitate formation while also stating that the alloy should not be converted into a multiphase alloy. Nanoprecipitates ordinarily constitute a second phase unless they are explicitly defined as same-phase compositional modulations; that distinction is not provided.
